name: Western Krahn
confidence_why: One first-hand description of the tone system, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Duitsman, John. 1986. Testing two systems for marking tone in Western Krahn. Notes on Literacy 49: 2-10. Dallas: SIL.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.A 'Western Krahn system', re-edition pp. 1-2; last two sentences from Appendix 'Tone lesson—diacritic system' step 3, p. 8
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

tone_statements.citation: Duitsman, John. 1986. Testing two systems for marking tone in Western Krahn. Notes on Literacy (SIL) 2-10; and Ingemann, Frances, John Duitsman & Will Doe. 1972. A survey of Krahn dialects in Liberia. University of Liberia Journal.
tone_statements.quote: The present Western Krahn tone-marking system utilizes four diacritics written over vowels: v́ High tone kó ‘frog’ v̄ Mid tone k ōō ‘mongoose’ v̀ Low tone kòò ‘bath house’ v̌ Rising tone k ǒ ‘chalk’ ... Ask students to give other examples of these four tones. Make four lists, one for each of the four tones.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.A 'Western Krahn system', re-edition pp. 1-2; last two sentences from Appendix 'Tone lesson—diacritic system' step 3, p. 8
tone_statements.summary: Orthography-testing paper: four tones (high, mid, low, rising) written as diacritics over vowels; no phonological analysis, TBU, downstep or stress. Spaces in 'k ōō', 'k ǒ' are the reprint's setting.

sources.citation: Bing, Janet Mueller & John Duitsman. 1993. Postpositions and the valency marker in Krahn: monosemy versus polysemy. Journal of West African Languages 23(1): 91-104.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.3.35)
sources.note: Silent on stress. Phonological preliminaries p. 92: 'The tonal systems of Krahn are complex and consist of rising and falling as well as level tones' (tones numbered 1 highest to 4 lowest; nasalization is a word-level suprasegmental; clitics belong to the phonological word). Footnote 3: 'Gbaeson tone is described in Duitsman (1978)'. Data from Gbaeson and Gborbo dialects (both Western Krahn).

sources.citation: Bing, Janet Mueller. 1991. Color terms and lexical classes in Krahn/Wobé. Studies in African Linguistics 22(3): 277-296.
sources.note: Silent on stress; footnote 2 (p. 278) only: 'Numbers refer to phonemic tones with 1 indicating the highest, 4 the lowest, and combinations indicating contour tone (see Bing [1993b] and Bearth & Link [1980])'. Gborbo dialect.

sources.citation: Bearth, Thomas & Christa Link. 1980. The tone puzzle of Wobé. Studies in African Linguistics 11(2): 147-207.
sources.note: Sister variety Wobé (Wè Northern, weno1238; Tao dialect), not Western Krahn: 14 contrasting tones on short monosyllables, syllable shape C1(C2)V1(V2)(V3); vowel length noted; no statement on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Duitsman, John, Jana Bertkau & James Laesch. 1975. A survey of Kru dialects. Studies in African Linguistics 6(1): 77-103.
sources.note: About Kru/Klao, with Krahn only as comparison; sec. 4.4 Tone: 'Phonetically, there are three level tones and, in most dialects, at least one rising and at least one falling tone. As in Krahn, there is an amazing amount of tonal interaction between syllables'. No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Bing, Janet. 1993. Default features in contour tones: evidence from Krahn/Wobe. In M. Eid & G. Iverson (eds.), Principles and Prediction: The Analysis of Natural Language (CILT 98), 327-338. Amsterdam: Benjamins.

sources.note: Tonal analysis of Gborbo Krahn cited by Bing 1991 and Bing & Duitsman 1993 for the tone system.

tone.says: Argues from Krahn/Wobé contour tones for default (underspecified) tone features; a dedicated tonal-phonology paper; whether Wobé forms are analysed directly is unseen.
